Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Overview 2 Turn 3 Card Distribution 4 Round End 5 Round Scoring 6 Game End Overview Have the LOWEST score. [ Fast Tutorial ] Turn Place a card from your hand onto the previously played card. If your card is ... lower value, end your turn. higher value, draw a new card then end your turn. same value, play again. Card Distribution 8 blue cards (4 per 0 and 1 value) 15 green cards (5 per 2, 3 and 4 value) 18 yellow cards (6 per 5, 6 and 7 value) 21 orange cards (7 per 8, 9 and 10 value) 16 red cards (8 per 11 and 12 value) Round End When a player has three cards or fewer at their turn end, they trigger round end. (If there are two players, "two or fewer cards".) That player places their remaining cards facedown in front of them. The remaining players continue to play, but if anyone else reaches three or less cards they do the same. If it comes round to a player with no hand cards, they instead reveal a facedown card. When a player reveals their final facedown card, this is the end of a round and that player takes the Mojo card. Then all players reveal their remaining facedown cards. Round Scoring Your score is calculated with the cards in front of you and with the cards in your hand. Out of all of these, for each color take your highest number, then add together your highest value of each color and this is your score. If you hold the Mojo and your score is the lowest score or equal to the lowest score, then score 0 points instead of your calculated score. If you hold the Mojo and someone else has a lower score than you, gain 10 points to your score. Turn the Mojo to the 0 or +10 side as rewarded, then place it back in the center to start a new round (this determines turn order). Unless the game end is triggered, play a new round. Game End The game ends when a player reaches or exceeds 50 points. The player(s) with the lowest points, wins! [Rating: 1/10] Played this one a dozen or so times. It feels like it is just on the verge of being a nice light card game. There are several redeeming qualities: the minimal rule set, the anticipation of the rise and fall of the discard values, and the timing of when to go out. But instead the emphasis on card draw luck (both in opening hands and subsequent draws) makes it almost a parody of these types of games. If you find yourself reaching for Mojo, do yourself a favour and go play L.L.A.M.A. or Scout instead.

[Rating: 1/10] This reminds me of a game I used to play when young, some 30 years ago, using a standard deck of cards. We used to shuffle 2 decks of 52 cards together and have 3 cards in the centre. So not sure this is an original game or a derivative of an old game.  When you first play and learn the basic strategy you get dragged in thinking the game has some skill. But sadly not, the game is pure luck. You can have the most amazing hand and through no fault of your own keep picking up 12 when you trying to get out. [Rating: 1/10] UNO variant shedding game. Still not enough here to draw interest although would work for casuals.

[Rating: 2/10] Wavered back and forth on whether I like this game. And after so menu played in BGA I think it's just a glorified Uno that tried to be smarter. If you dump a 12 and get a low number it's fun. After a 20 times not getting what you want or setting someone else up to dump their whole lucky hand it's not much fun. I'll be happy to never think about this game again.

[Rating: 3/10] Like UNO with all of the non-number cards removed. Definitely not for me, as this is not what I am looking for in a party game, but I can see fans of this type of game being into this one.  .

[Rating: 3/10] For every three hands you outplay your opponents, you'll get one hand that undoes everything. It's wildly unpredictable and lacks a certain tactical appreciation, but then Kevin yells, "I've lost my Mojo!" and I almost forget about all of that.

[Rating: 3/10] Played on BGA.  Simple card tosser where the strategy becomes pretty simple after a play or 2.
